method: Each record's cited URL was captured with tools/capture.py (never WebFetch) and compared byte-for-byte, whitespace-normalised only, against (a) the record's own snippet and (b) every quote a card profile draws from that record. The record's claim was then judged against the captured page. Records were NOT patched to fit their pages: a contradicted record is left as it is, because the contradiction is the finding.
scope: the 46 search-only records that docs/reference/cards/*.json actually cite -- not the whole corpus

outcome_meaning.A_verified: snippet verbatim on the page AND the page supports the claim; record upgraded to fetched
outcome_meaning.B_snippet_off: the page supports the claim, but the snippet/quote is not verbatim on it -- usually search-engine truncation or splicing, sometimes invented detail around a real fact
outcome_meaning.C_contradicted: the page does not support the claim: either silent on it, or asserting the opposite
outcome_meaning.D_unreachable: the cited page was never actually retrieved, so nothing is proven either way. NOT evidence of a defect.

caveat_arxiv: capture.py routes every arxiv.org/{abs,pdf,html} URL to the Atom API, which returns title+abstract only. For arXiv-sourced records, absence from the abstract is NOT absence from the paper. Those are filed D_unreachable, never C_contradicted.

profile_quotes.quote: ACP standardizes AI agent interaction (prompts, sessions, file permissions, streaming) between editors and coding agents.
After LSP, one language server worked everywhere. ACP does the same for AI agents.

records.evidence_from_page: The Agent Client Protocol (ACP) is a JSON-RPC 2.0 standard that lets any AI coding agent run inside any supporting editor... Think LSP, but for AI agents instead of language servers. ... ACP fixes this with a simple idea borrowed from LSP: define a standard wire protocol between editors and agents, so any agent can plug into any editor.
records.notes: Neither the record's snippet nor either profile quote appears anywhere on the page (verified: the terms 'streaming', 'permission', 'autocomplete', 'language features', 'closest analogy', and 'one language server worked everywhere' do not occur anywhere in the 18,932-char capture) -- so both TEST1 and TEST2 fail and the two quotes card 3.1 relies on are not on this page. But claim_to_test itself ('ACP is the LSP equivalent for AI agents...') IS genuinely supported by real page text -- 'Think LSP, but for AI agents instead of language servers' and 'ACP fixes this with a simple idea borrowed from LSP: define a standard wire protocol between editors and agents, so any agent can plug into any editor' say the same thing in different, terser words. So per TEST3 (claim support, the outcome-deciding test) this is B not C: snippet/quotes are an embellished paraphrase carrying invented specifics (the 'prompts, sessions, file permissions, streaming' enumeration and the LSP 'autocomplete, go-to-definition' gloss appear nowhere on the page), not a fabrication of the underlying fact. Correct verbatim replacement for re-sourcing: 'Think LSP, but for AI agents instead of language servers.' (TL;DR) plus 'ACP fixes this with a simple idea borrowed from LSP: define a standard wire protocol between editors and agents, so any agent can plug into any editor.' (body).

profile_quotes.quote: Zed introduced ACP in August 2025, and JetBrains joined shortly after.

records.evidence_from_page: The analogy people reach for is Language Server Protocol (LSP), and it is a useful one: ACP aims to break the old 1:1 coupling where each editor needed a bespoke integration for each agent. Zed introduced ACP in August 2025, and JetBrains joined shortly after. That quickly turned ACP from a Zed-specific integration mechanism into a broader interoperability layer for agentic coding workflows.
records.notes: Snippet and the card 3.1 quote are both verbatim on the page, in context, unambiguously supporting the claim. This is the ONLY record in this lane whose profile-relied-on quote survives verbatim. Record updated: status -> fetched, fetch_tool -> service, read -> verbatim excerpt including one sentence of lead-in context. No other fields touched. Edit already appears in HEAD with a clean working tree per git status -- that is environment snapshotting between tool calls in this sandbox, not an action I took; I never ran git commit or tools/checkpoint.sh.

profile_quotes.quote: For a local agent, the editor launches it as a subprocess and they talk JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio.

records.evidence_from_page: The protocol works like this: 1. The editor (client) spawns the agent as a subprocess 2. The agent communicates back over JSON-RPC 2.0 on stdin/stdout (local agents) or HTTP/WebSocket (remote agents, still in development) 3. Work organizes into sessions (a conversation with shared context) and turns (individual prompt-response cycles) 4. The agent can request file access, terminal execution, and tool calls, all through the protocol
records.notes: The core claim (editor spawns agent as subprocess; local agents talk JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdin/stdout) is genuinely supported by the page, just worded differently ('spawns...as a subprocess' vs 'launches it as a subprocess'; 'on stdin/stdout' vs 'over stdio'). However the second half of the record's snippet/claim -- 'No ports, no daemons' -- does not appear anywhere on the page at all (checked: 'daemon' and 'No ports' both absent from the full capture) and is an unsourced editorial addition, same pattern as X-cap-agent-runtime-002 above (same source URL). Correct verbatim replacement sentence for re-sourcing: 'The editor (client) spawns the agent as a subprocess' + 'The agent communicates back over JSON-RPC 2.0 on stdin/stdout (local agents) or HTTP/WebSocket (remote agents, still in development)'. Left unchanged per instructions (status stays search-only).

records.evidence_from_page: This is a Nov 8, 2023 Greg Dennis blog post 'Interpreting JSON Schema Output.' Its whole subject is why a PASSING validation can still contain output nodes marked invalid (if/then/else and anyOf/oneOf semantics) -- e.g. 'looking at the validation output for the second instance...we notice that the output node for the /if subschema has valid: false. It does use fields named evaluationPath/schemaLocation/instanceLocation (which are JSON-Pointer-shaped) and its 'List format' example does show multiple detail nodes on one level -- a weak, indirect partial-support thread -- but the record's specific claim (single-pass reporting, RFC 6901 framing) is not made anywhere on the page.
records.notes: Snippet and both quoted sentences are absent verbatim. Page is real, reachable, and on-topic (JSON Schema output) but is not about the claim it is cited for -- it's about interpreting seemingly-contradictory valid/invalid subschema nodes, a different question. claim_verdict is 'silent' rather than 'contradicts': nothing on the page asserts the opposite of single-pass reporting, it simply never raises the topic. profile_quotes.quote: LangGraph checkpoints turn a graph into a durable program: after every super-step the full state is snapshotted to a Checkpointer (in-memory, SQLite, or Postgres), keyed by thread_id

records.evidence_from_page: 'Persistence writes a "checkpoint" to a database or file every time the graph moves to a new node... By giving every action a thread_id, LangGraph keeps different users and tasks separate. When you resume a thread, the agent picks up where it left off. It reconstructs its internal state from the last checkpoint.' and 'MemorySaver stores checkpoints in the computer's RAM, so data is lost when the program stops. PostgresSaver stores checkpoints in a PostgreSQL database, allowing state to persist across restarts.' and 'LangGraph persistence supports "time travel." By using the thread_id and a specific checkpoint_id, you can inspect previous states, fork the conversation, or even restart from a middle point.'
